paper_title: CRISP: Cliff-awaRe Input-adaptive Sparse Prefilling with Structural-Mass-Motivated Routing

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: The attention prefilling phase of long-context LLM inference scales quadratically, making self-attention a severe computational bottleneck. Traditional sparse attention methods mitigate this through fixed patterns or offline profiling, but lack the flexibility to adapt to input-dependent attention structure. Recent dynamic methods address this by routing heads to sparse patterns in real-time, but rely on indirect routing proxies with overhead and budget allocation mechanisms that overlook the post-softmax mass hierarchy. We present CRISP (Cliff-awaRe Input-adaptive Sparse Prefilling), which identifies and addresses two structural challenges in this dynamic routing paradigm. First, we show that the routing decision can be read directly off the structure of the proxy attention map. We replace the Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JSD) routing with C_struct, a structural proxy that measures mass at Vertical-Slash compatible positions and reproduces JSD's routing decisions while eliminating both the pooled matmul and subsequent KL divergence overhead. Second, we formalize the post-softmax mass cliff and demonstrate theoretically that strictly cumulative coverage thresholds accumulate O(n) background noise at long contexts. CRISP navigates this via a sink-aware threshold grounded in the noise floor. Empirically, across InfiniteBench, RULER and LongBench on two model families, CRISP is the strongest sparse method overall and matches or exceeds exact dense attention on retrieval-heavy benchmarks, recovering up to +28.0 pp on retrieval tasks over baselines and achieving up to a 5.30x attention speedup at 512k tokens, driven primarily by our O(n) noise elimination during selection while preserving structural integrity.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: The prefilling phase of long-context LLM inference scales quadratically, making self-attention severe bottleneck. Traditional sparse attention uses fixed patterns (Child et al., 2019; Zaheer et al., 2020) or offline profiling (Jiang et al., 2024), lacking the flexibility to adapt to input-dependent attention structures. To address this, state-of-the-art methods like FlexPrefill (Lai et al., 2025) introduce dynamic routing, categorizing heads in realtime to allocate compute budgets. Specifically, it uses Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JSD) for pattern routing and cumulative coverage threshold γ for index selection. However, analyzing their theoretical foundations reveals principled limitations in both mechanisms. JSD is an indirect routing signal. FlexPrefill sends each head down one of two paths: VerticalSlash (VS) for heads whose attention is sharply concentrated, Pooled-Estimation (PE) for heads whose attention is spread out. What the router needs is therefore cheap read on how concentrated head is. JSD obtains one indirectly, by building second, pooled estimate of the heads attention and measuring how far it diverges from the per-query one, routing to VS above threshold τ . That estimate exists only for the comparison, and costs matmul and softmax that nothing else in the method needs. We take shortcut instead: in these models concentrated head places its mass at structurally predictable positionsthe attention sinks and the local recency windowso the mass sitting there is itself read on concentration. Cstruct measures exactly that, costs nothing beyond what index selection already computes, and agrees with JSDs routing decision on 94.0% (Llama) and 88.1% (Qwen) of measured heads. Cumulative thresholds cannot navigate the mass cliff. On VS heads, softmax amplification produces rigid mass hierarchy: architectural sinks (might absorb up to > 90% mass), task-relevant signal blocks, and near-zero background noise (Deng et al., 2024). We term the sharp boundary beFigure 1: Post-softmax attention mass distribution, illustrating the two opposite failure modes of cumulative thresholding (γ=0.95). Left (sink-only collapse): high sink mass causes γ=0.95 to terminate inside the sink, leaving important blocks unreached. Right (noise accumulation): when sink mass is distributed, γ=0.95 exhausts the important band and accumulates 13 noise blocks. The CRISP noise-floor (α=1.0, dotted purple) correctly separates signal from noise in both cases. Additional head examples are provided in Appendix D. tween signal and noise the mass cliff. Cumulative γ-thresholding accumulates mass indiscriminately across this boundary, producing two inherent structural failure modes depending on where γ falls relative to the sink mass: sink-only collapse, in which selection terminates before reaching signal, and residual noise accumulation, in which O(n) near-zero background tokens are collected to satisfy the residual threshold. Tuning γ cannot resolve this: increasing coverage merely pushes selection deeper into noise. We replace γ on VS heads with sink-aware threshold grounded in the noise floor, which explicitly separates signal from architectural noise without empirical calibration. Contributions. (1) We give structural account of VS/PE routing and show empirically that FlexPrefills JSD signal tracks the same headlevel distinction (3). (2) We introduce Cstruct, structural-mass proxy that removes the matmul and KL divergence required by JSD-based routing while reproducing its decisions (3.2). (3) We identify the post-softmax mass cliff and provide an asymptotic analysis showing that coverage-based thresholds inherently accumulate O(n) noise at scale (4). (4) We introduce CRISP, method using sink-aware thresholding that achieves parity with dense attention and provides up to 5.30 speedups, driven entirely by resolving the O(n) noise accumulation bottleneck (5).

sections.title: 3 Structural-Mass Routing
sections.content: The routing decision follows from simple observation about attention entropy. The informationtheoretic link between entropy and support size (Campbell, 1966) tells us that low-entropy heads need few tokens for high coverage. consistent finding across prior work is that in autoregressive transformers, these tokens occupy structurally predictable positionsarchitectural sinks (Xiao et al., 2024), vertical columns, and slash diagonals (Jiang et al., 2024; Lai et al., 2025)giving rise to the Vertical-Slash pattern that sparse methods exploit. Low-entropy heads are therefore well-suited to the VS path, which captures these patterns at fine granularity. High-entropy heads lack such structure: mass is spread broadly with no dominant pattern for VS to exploit, making pooled estimation (PE) the more effective strategy. This account motivates the routing dichotomy itself; it does not by itself say which computable quantity should decide it. 3.1 examines what FlexPrefills JSD signal measures in practice, and 3.2 replaces it with structural quantity that is already available. The structural half of this account mass at sinks and recencyis property of current sink-having architectures, not of softmax attention in general (See Appendix for the informationtheoretic grounding of the dichotomy). 3.1 What JSD Measures FlexPrefill routes on JSD(a, ˆa), the divergence between the pooled estimate (softmax applied after pooling queries and keys) and the per-query mean ˆa (averaging after softmax); these two constructions do not agree in general, and it is their disagreement that the routing consumes. Empirically the disagreement is large exactly on the concentrated heads and small on the diffuse ones, which is what makes it usable for routingbut this is measured regularity of these models, not consequence of any property of softmax. The vertical and slash components of VS head contribute to it very differently, which offers an intuition for why. Where queries agree on the same keysthe vertical casepooling before the softmax and averaging after it yield nearly the same distribution, and the divergence is small. Where queries peak on different keysthe slash casethe two orders come apart: pooling first concentrates on whichever key carries the largest cross-query mean, whereas averaging after leaves ˆa spread across the keys individual queries prefer, so the estimates place their mass on different supports and the divergence is large even though every query row is itself concentrated. Because both structures co-occur in real VS heads, it is the slash component that drives JSD above τ , while diffuse PE heads produce little divergence from either. We offer this as an observation consistent with our measurements rather than as derivation. sections.title: 4 Navigating the Mass Cliff
sections.content: 4.1 The Post-Softmax Token Hierarchy On VS heads, softmax creates three-class hierarchy separated by hard cliff: Architectural Sinks often absorb dominant portion of the total mass; Task-Relevant Signal holds moderate above-baseline mass; Background Noise carries near-zero mass that diminishes with sequence lengthsoftmax normalization distributes background mass across tokens, yielding per-token mass ϵ that scales as O(1/n) for fixed presoftmax gap. This is consistent with the theoretical framework of Deng et al. (2024), which confirms that attention is naturally sparse. 4.2 The O(n) Scaling Limitations of γ Early work established that attention sparsity must be dynamic and input-dependent rather than static (Liu et al., 2021). To implement this dynamic routing, recent methods mathematically formulate index selection as constrained dual-optimization problem: minimizing subset size subject to cumulative coverage constraint, (cid:80) aj γ (Lai et al., 2025). However, this specific optimization objective assumes all attention mass is semantically equivalent. By failing to account for the postsoftmax token hierarchy, strictly cumulative formulations overlook the mass cliff, resulting in two inherent structural failure modes at scale: Sink-Only Collapse. When asink γ, selection terminates before any task-relevant tokens are evaluated. The error bound is formally satisfied, but the selected set contains zero semantic information. Residual Noise Accumulation. When asink + aimportant < γ, the algorithm crosses the cliff into background noise, collecting O(γresidual/ϵ) O(n) noise tokens (see Appendix C). γ-tuning cannot escape the cliff. Figure 1 illustrates both failure modes empirically. These are Figure 4: Attention-only latency scaling (64k512k tokens, single H100, mean std shading on FP baselines only for clarity). Left: absolute latency; FP variance explodes at long contexts due to input-dependent cliff position, while all three CRISP configurations scale tightly. Right: speedup over FlashAttention; all CRISP configurations overtake their FlexPrefill counterparts beyond 131k, reaching 5.17, 5.30, and 5.40 at 512k for α{1.0, 1.25, 1.5} respectively. increasing γ crosses parametrically irreparable: the cliff deeper into noise. Table 2 confirms thisγ=0.97 degrades some benchmarks while marginally improving others, with inconsistent effects across models and tasks. This is precisely what the mass cliff predicts: the effect depends on where sink mass falls relative to the threshold, not on coverage quality. CRISP avoids this dependency by grounding selection in the noise floor rather than coverage target. 4.3 Fix: Sink-Aware Thresholding Throughout, the proxy attention map is partitioned into Nb = n/B blocks of B=128 tokens, so the anchor windows of 3.2 (wsink = wlocal = 128) are exactly the first and last block. We exclude these always-retained blocksthe first block (architectural sinks) and the last block (local recency, always retained following FlexPrefill)and establish baseline expected mass over the remaining Nb 2 blocks: µ = max(1 afirst alast, 0) Nb 2 (3) tasks select more. Unlike γ, the threshold correctly lowers µ as sinks grow, maintaining sensitivity to signal regardless of sink mass. Note that for high-entropy PE heads, mass is diffuse and lacks sharp structural hierarchy. Consequently, PE heads do not suffer from the same severe mass cliff as VS heads, allowing CRISP to safely retain γ-cumsum approximation for the PE path without accumulating disproportionate noise (Algorithm 4); Appendix shows the corresponding mass profiles. What does not change is the decomposition itself. CRISP still computes both directions: the vertical score av (column means of ˆA) and the slash score as (diagonal means) are still computed separately, thresholded separately, and unioned into single block index set (Algorithm 3; cf. Algorithm 6 in Appendix A). What changes is the budget rule applied within each direction: the cumulative criterion (cid:80) aj γ is replaced by the noise floor αµd, so the number of selected blocks follows from how many blocks carry above-background mass rather than from coverage target. block is selected if and only if it exceeds the expected background mass:

sections.title: 6 Related Work
sections.content: Fixed and Offline Sparse Attention. Early sparse attention methods employ fixed structural patterns, including Sparse Transformers (Child et al., 2019), global-local combinations as in BigBird (Zaheer et al., 2020) and Longformer (Beltagy et al., 2020), sliding window attention (Jiang et al., 2023), and the attention sink mechanism of StreamingLLM (Xiao et al., 2024), which combines initial-token sinks with local sliding window. MInference (Jiang et al., 2024) advances beyond purely fixed patterns by profiling per-head sparse patterns offline and generating dynamic indices at runtime within those profiles. However, offline pattern assignment cannot adapt to inputdependent variation in sink mass: when mass concentration changes across inputs or context lengths, fixed profile either over-selects sinks or underselects signal. This limitation is quantified in our experiments, where MInference trails FlexPrefill by 58 pp on LongBench and collapses on longcontext RULERconstituting empirical evidence that the mass cliff requires online navigation. Dynamic Sparse Attention. FlexPrefill (Lai et al., 2025) represents the current state of the art in dynamic sparse attention by routing heads and allocating budgets at prefill time based on each inputs attention structure. Other recent approaches dynamically select tokens by tracking heavy hitters during generation (Zhang et al., 2023), utilize query-aware page routing (Tang et al., 2024), route heads to mixture of sparse attention patterns (Fu et al., 2025), approximate attention scores via query-component slicing (Ribar et al., 2024), or employ locality-sensitive hashing for importance sampling (Chen et al., 2025). Concurrently, Twilight (Lin et al., 2025) replaces fixed top-k budgets with top-p pruning that adaptively selects the minimum token set whose attention weights exceed cumulative threshold, addressing the over/underselection problem inherent in static budgets during decoding. Its scope is complementary to ours rather than overlapping: Twilight operates on single query row at decode time and targets KVcache memory bandwidth, whereas CRISP operates on the full prefill attention map and targets compute-bound cost, so the two could in principle be composed (CRISP for prefilling, Twilight for decoding). Separately, Nawrot et al. (2026) provide large-scale isoCost analysis showing that sparse attention efficiency varies dramatically across task types, with aggregation and multi-hop tasks degrading at sparsity levels that retrieval tasks tolerate consistent with our finding that cumulative thresholding fails to preserve task-relevant signal at scale. as Mamba (Gu and Dao, 2024), gated linear attention such as Gated DeltaNet (Yang et al., 2025), and post-hoc linearization of pretrained Transformers, as in LoLCATs (Zhang et al., 2025a) and Lizard (Nguyen et al., 2026). These change the architecture and usually require distillation or finetuning, whereas CRISP is training-free and computes exact softmax attention on the blocks it selects; the two directions are complementary. Theoretical grounding for the routing dichotomy between structured and diverse attention heads has remained limited: Likhosherstov et al. (2021) implicitly connected attention concentration to representational capacity, and Zhang et al. (2025b) established attention entropy as key factor governing parallel context encoding efficiency, but without formal account of the VS/PE dichotomy or its interaction with cumulative thresholding. The present work provides that foundation, identifying the mass cliff as an intrinsic structural consequence of autoregressive softmax attention and proving that strictly cumulative coverage criterion (Lai et al., 2025) is asymptotically ill-suited to ultra-long contexts.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: We identified and resolved two principled limitations in dynamic sparse attention. First, we replaced indirect JSD-based routing with Cstruct, structural-mass proxy that reproduces JSDs routing decisions while eliminating the pooling matmul and KL divergence overhead. Second, we formalised the post-softmax mass cliff, proving that cumulative γ-thresholding inherently accumulates O(n) background noise. By implementing sink-aware noise-floor threshold, CRISP explicitly separates signal from architectural noise. Consequently, CRISP establishes new performance hierarchy, recovering up to +28.0 pp on retrieval tasks, achieving parity with exact dense attention on InfiniteBench, and delivering up to 5.30 latency speedup at 512k tokens. Ultimately, navigating the mass cliff provides robust, theoretically grounded foundation for scaling long-context sparse attention.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Subquadratic Alternatives. parallel line of work removes the quadratic cost rather than sparsifying it, replacing softmax attention with linear or recurrent formulations: state-space models such Architectural Scope. Cstruct is structural measurement, not formal entropy quantity, and it works as routing signal because low-entropy heads in current sink-having architectures concentrate their mass at sinks and recency  (Table 1)  . This is an empirical property of the models we study, not guarantee. Architectures that suppress attention sinksfor instance via gated attentionbreak that correspondence, and CRISPs assumptions do not hold there. Sparse attention in the sink-free regime is largely unexplored, and the prior methods we compare against (Jiang et al., 2024; Lai et al., 2025) do not address it either; the entropy argument for the VS/PE dichotomy itself (Appendix B) is property of softmax attention and would still apply in principle, but different structural proxy would be required. Our evidence spans two model families at 78B scale, which bounds how far these regularities should be assumed to generalise. Hybrid Heads. CRISP inherits FlexPrefills binary VS/PE routing. Real heads are not always cleanly one or the other: some carry mixed structure, and forcing such head onto the VS path lets the sink-aware threshold discard tokens that do not fit that pattern. Softer schemesprobabilistic mixing, or per-head confidence-weighted decisions are left to future work. Scaling and Decoding. Empirical verification on models > 8B or contexts beyond established benchmarks remains future work. Additionally, this addresses prefilling only; extension to tokenlevel decoding under causal masking requires characterizing the mass cliff dynamically during autoregressive generation. Path Selection. CRISP improvements focus heavily on the VS path. While PE heads lack sharp mass cliff hierarchy, full improvements to the PE path and dynamic scheduling of α to mitigate precision-coverage tradeoffs in aggregation tasks (e.g., Llama RULER) are left to future treatment.

Between these extremes, concentrating mass on fewer tokens (lowering entropy) reduces the number of tokens needed for coverage γ, so low-entropy heads require compact index sets while high-entropy heads require broad coverage. Connection to routing. For low-entropy heads (eH(a) n), compact sparse index set suffices. Prior work has consistently observed that in autoregressive transformers, low-entropy heads concentrate mass at structurally predictable positions sinks, vertical columns, and slash diagonals (Xiao et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2024; Lai et al., 2025) making the VS path natural fit. For highentropy heads (eH(a) n), the required support is large and no compact structural pattern dominates; pooled estimation over the full sequence is more appropriate. CRISP replaces Algorithm 5 with constant-time indexed slice reduction over ˆA (eliminating the O(nd/b) pooled matmul and O(n/b) KL divergence overhead in Lines 3-5), and replaces Algorithm 6 with blocklevel sink-aware thresholding (eliminating the dualdirection decomposition in Lines 25). Entropy-Coverage Relationship We provide the information-theoretic intuition underlying the VS/PE routing dichotomy. Effective support size. The exponentiated entropy eH(a) is the standard information-theoretic measure of the effective support size of distribution (Campbell, 1966). At the two extremes: Concentrated: H(a) 0 eH(a) 1. single element holds most mass; coverage γ is achieved with very few tokens. Uniform: H(a) = log eH(a) = n. This is consistent with the general sparsity framework of Deng et al. (2024).

sections.title: D Additional Mass Cliff Examples
sections.content: Figure 5 provides additional visual examples of the post-softmax mass cliff across four entirely different layers and heads of Llama-3.1-8B. These further demonstrate the two structural failure modes of cumulative γ-thresholding. Wherever the cliff falls for given head, the CRISP noise-floor criterion (α=1.0) isolates the task-relevant signal without accumulating O(n) background noise. Figure 5: Extended visualization of the post-softmax attention mass distribution across four additional representative VS heads. Both failure modes (sink-only collapse and noise accumulation) arise from the same fixed threshold applied to heads whose cliff sits at different positions, indicating that the failure is structural limitation of cumulative thresholding rather than calibration artefact. These panels show cross-head heterogeneity at fixed input; we do not claim from them that single heads cliff moves across inputs.

sections.title: E Hyperparameter Robustness
sections.content: Tables 6 and 7 report sensitivity to the two CRISP hyperparameters, α and τproxy, on Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B respectively. Performance degrades monotonically as α increases above 1.0, confirming that raising the threshold past the noise floor progressively discards signal. Notably, α=0.75 performs comparably to α=1.0, matching or exceeding it on some benchmarks (e.g., Qwen LongBench). This is expected: lower α retains more blocks, benefiting tasks that require broader coverage at the cost of admitting some near-threshold noise. The noise floor is thus better understood as stable region rather than knifeedgevalues in [0.75, 1.0] all correctly separate signal from deep background noise, differing only in how aggressively they treat borderline blocks. We recommend α=1.0 as the default because it is the only value with calibration-free interpretation (above-average residual mass), removing the need for per-task tuning. Even at α=1.5well beyond the principled defaultCRISP still Paretodominates FlexPrefill γ=0.95 on aggregate accuracy while running faster (Figure 3), demonstrating graceful degradation. Critically, τproxy sensitivity is low: varying τproxy {0.15, 0.2, 0.25} produces spread of less than 0.7pp on InfiniteBench and less than 1.2pp on LongBench across both model families, with no single value dominating uniformly. This insensitivity confirms that Cstruct provides stable routing signal across wide threshold range, requiring no careful per-model calibration. No single value dominates uniformly across benchmarks and models; the spread across the full range is 1.2pp, confirming that Cstruct routing is robust to threshold choice and requires no per-model calibration. Why the PE Path Keeps γ-cumsum 4.3 argues that PE heads do not exhibit the mass cliff and can therefore retain γ-cumsum. Figure 6 supports that empirically, using the same Llama3.1-8B block-mass dump that produces Figures 1 and 5. We identify diffuse heads by their top-1 block mass, drawing four from different layers. Their profiles decay gently and monotonically with no boundary anywhere: the noise floor sits inside the bulk of the distribution rather than at step, which is exactly the regime in which mean-based threshold has nothing to separate. The concentration statistic makes the same point numericallythe top-50 blocks hold only 15% to 80% of these heads mass, against 99% for the VS head shown for contrast, whose sink block alone carries 0.929. Cumulative thresholding does not over-collect here because there is no near-zero background band to fall into: γ=0.95 is not even reached within the top 50 blocks. Accumulating to coverage therefore selects representative subset rather than disproportionate residual, which is why replacing it would gain nothing on this path. Two caveats. The dump stores each heads top50 block masses sorted by magnitude, so it characterises concentration and does not let us recompute the routing decision itself; we identify these heads as diffuse, and rely on the measured 91.3% rate at which top-1 mass sits at an anchor position  (Table 1)  to connect low concentration to low Cstruct and hence to the PE path. The dump also covers single model and input, so this establishes the shape of the PE-head distribution, not its variability. Per-Benchmark Pareto Plots Figure 3(a) aggregates three benchmarks and two models into one point per method, which hides taskspecific behaviour. Figure 7 separates them. CRISP α=1.0 leads on InfiniteBench and LongBench, but on RULER it sits marginally below both FlexPrefill settings on the Llama sidethe precision-coverage tradeoff discussed in 5.2. We show it here rather than leaving it inside an average.
